title: Adverse effect of LRBA ban may be reality
full_text:
The SMSF Association is expecting the sector to have to deal with unintended consequences from the decision to use the definition of business real property as a key factor in how the limited recourse borrowing arrangement (LRBA) rule change will now apply.
“[The definition of business real property] was designed for a different purpose, [but] now we’re using it to determine whether someone meets the requirements of an LRBA,” SMSF Association chief executive Peter Burgess told delegates at the ASF Audits Technical Conference 2026 recently held in Adelaide.
“[As such, issues will arise] where if a property stops being leased at some point, does it mean [the asset] no longer meets the [business real property] definition?”
Burgess indicated the industry body is hoping the ATO takes a pragmatic approach to this type of situation and others like it, but recognised the nature of the policy may prevent this from happening.
“It was a quick fix or quick amendment that it made and there are going to be some unintended consequences as a result that we are all going to have to deal with,” he said.
ASF Audits head of technical Jo Hurley took the opportunity to criticise the change to the LRBA rules, labelling it as a move that restricts SMSF member strategies when looking to include residential property in their fund portfolios.
“The reality for clients is that LRBAs can provide an opportunity for diversification which is actually a risk-reduction strategy. Without the gearing, property can represent quite a significant percentage of fund assets, particularly in funds starting out,” Hurley explained.
Burgess concurred and said this impact of the rule change was particularly unsatisfactory.
“That was the disappointing thing from our point of view because it takes away an option that some people [have to include residential property in their fund because typically] they haven’t been able to invest in residential property; they don’t have enough money outside of superannuation to be able to do it,” he said.
“So this [amendment] is now taking away that option they otherwise had and it may be the only option they have to invest in residential property.”
